nuevos.titulo_original: Should Adults Take Choline?
nuevos.descripcion:
Should adults be taking choline supplements? It helps to know what happens when you go without it.

In 1991, researchers admitted healthy men to hospital, and half of them went without choline. Within three weeks, their blood choline fell by about 30%, and a liver enzyme that signals liver damage started to climb. The body uses choline to build the outer wall of every cell and to make acetylcholine, a brain chemical messenger involved in memory and attention, which nerves also use to move muscles. Choline also supplies small chemical tags called methyl groups that help switch genes on and off.

Studies like this led to choline being officially recognized in 1998 as an essential nutrient, and most adults fall short of the recommended amount.

Does extra choline help adults? In Finland, men who ate the most phosphatidylcholine, the main form of choline in food, had about a 28% lower risk of dementia over 22 years, though total choline intake wasn't linked to dementia at all. That's an observational study, though: people who eat more eggs and fish differ in other ways. Trials in adults are small. One tested citicoline, a form of choline sold as a supplement, and found some improvements on memory tests in older adults, but it was run by the company that makes that supplement.

outliers.descripcion:
Te han dicho que la placa de tus arterias no se quita. Y en YouTube te venden que se disuelve con una taza de algo. Las dos cosas son falsas.

La placa aterosclerótica no es cal pegada a una tubería: es una herida de colesterol dentro de la pared de la arteria, cubierta por una tapa fibrosa. No se «limpia», pero sí se vacía. Los ensayos con ecografía intravascular lo miden desde hace 20 años: por encima de unos 80 mg/dL de LDL la placa crece; por debajo de 70, retrocede. Y cuanto más bajo, más retrocede. En SATURN, 2 de cada 3 pacientes consiguieron regresión. Cada 1 % de placa que se vacía se asocia a un 25 % menos de infartos, muertes y revascularizaciones.

En este vídeo te cuento cómo lo descubrimos (momias egipcias, soldados de 22 años, un cateterismo que salió mal y un moho de arroz), cuál es el número exacto al que tus arterias dan marcha atrás, por qué tu score de calcio puede SUBIR cuando lo estás haciendo bien, y qué hay detrás de los remedios que prometen «destapar» arterias en 30 días.

Nada de esto sustituye a tu médico: si tienes placa, pide tus cifras de LDL y ApoB y decide con él el objetivo.

outliers.descripcion:
Entrainment is one of the most powerful aspects of our biology.

Our circadian rhythm is created within us, but numerous studies show that our health is best when it is entrained to the rising and setting of the sun. That’s not to say you have to wake up at sunrise, but people who try to live nocturnally definitely suffer health consequences and people who match their sleep rhythm even somewhat to the rising and setting of the sun (one form of entrainment), derive many health benefits.

Entrainment works on shorter time scales too. Exercise at roughly the same time for a few days and you’ll notice your energy will increases a few minutes before that typical workout time.

Study or do some reading or some other form of work or learning at roughly the same time or times per day, and you’ll notice that your mental sharpness will start to increase in anticipation of those times.

To be clear, some of this is psychological, but a lot of it is physiological. The neuromodulators, hormones and neurotransmitters that regulate alertness and focus are readily susceptible to entrainment.

In this episode, Peter welcomes back Jeff Cavaliere, a physical therapist, strength coach, and founder of ATHLEAN-X who has spent decades bridging the gap between rehabilitation, athletic performance, and strength training. Jeff begins by sharing how his experience working with professional athletes and managing his own injuries has shaped his approach to building strength and muscle while minimizing injury risk. He discusses how training should evolve as we age, particularly for those in their 40s, 50s, and beyond who want to continue making progress without compromising long-term joint health. Jeff explains why excessive training volume can be counterproductive and how to balance reps in reserve with training to failure to maximize results while managing fatigue and injury risk. He also explores the differences between training for aesthetics and functional performance, explaining why these goals are not necessarily at odds. The conversation then shifts to a muscle-by-muscle breakdown of effective exercises for building strength and hypertrophy. Jeff highlights common training mistakes, offers modifications for those dealing with pain or injury, and explains why often-neglected muscles deserve more attention.
